lead: Yesterday Abram set out in great faith. Today, at the first hard test, he goes down to Egypt and gives way to fear, and God keeps the promise even so. The second reading sends Joshua back to Ai after his defeat, with the word “Do not fear”. Paul in the epistle teaches that everything rests on the God who shows mercy. In John, Jesus says that all he does comes from the Father. Taken together, the readings point away from our own strength: what God has begun depends on him, and on what the Son receives from the Father.

set: Abram has only just reached the land when a famine drives him out of it. Famine sent people from Canaan down to Egypt, whose food came from the yearly flood of the Nile. Genesis tells a like story twice more, of Abraham in Gerar (Genesis 20) and of Isaac (Genesis 26).

Many readers notice that this story runs ahead of the Exodus: famine, a going down to Egypt, danger to the family, plagues on Pharaoh, and a departure with great wealth. What will happen to the people happens first to their father.
str: vv. 9–10: from the Negeb to Egypt, because of famine.
vv. 11–13: Abram’s plan: “Say you are my sister”.
vv. 14–16: Sarai is taken to Pharaoh’s house, and Abram grows rich.
vv. 18–20: Pharaoh’s rebuke, and Abram is sent away.
kw: The word of v. 10. Abram goes as a foreigner without rights. He knows what it is to be a migrant in someone else’s land, and Israel’s law later remembers that experience (Exodus 22:21).
The half-truth of the story. Genesis 20:12 will say that Sarah was the daughter of Abraham’s father by another mother. Even so, the words here are meant to deceive.
Literally “blows” or “strokes”. Exodus 11:1 uses the same word for the last plague on Egypt.
vv: Now there was a famine in the land.
The land of promise greets Abram with hunger. Following God’s call does not remove trouble, and a true call can lead straight into difficulty.
Say you are my sister, so that it may go well with me because of you,

Yesterday’s man of faith is afraid for his life and puts his wife in danger. Abram did not ask God before he made this plan. The Bible does not hide the faults of its great figures, and that is one reason why it can be trusted.
What is this you have done to me?
The sharpest words in the passage come from a pagan king, who speaks the question of conscience to the man of promise. Abram has no answer, and the narrator gives him not a word.
ch: The promise stands because God keeps it, not because Abram is perfect. It is God who acts in v. 17 to protect Sarai, the mother of the promise. St Augustine, answering critics in Against Faustus 22, argued that Abraham concealed the truth rather than told a lie, since Sarah was his close kinswoman (in substance). The Catechism’s own teaching on lying is clear (CCC 2482–2486), and we need not defend every act of the patriarchs in order to honour their faith.

r.h: The Son does what he sees the Father doing
set: This is the start of Jesus’ reply to the charge that he made himself equal to God (5:18). The discourse runs to the end of the chapter. It does not deny the charge, but it explains it: the Son’s equality with the Father is a total dependence and communion. These verses are one of the clearest places in the Gospels for the relation of Father and Son.
str: v. 19: the principle: the Son does nothing on his own, and whatever the Father does, the Son does.
v. 20: the reason: love, and “greater works”.
vv. 21–22: two works that belong to God alone: giving life and judging.
v. 23: the purpose: the same honour for the Son.
kw: A double amen, found only in John. Jesus uses it to open a solemn teaching, and he speaks it on his own authority.
In Jewish faith, to raise the dead belongs to God. Jesus says that the Son shares this work.
The word used for the honour given to God. In v. 23 the same honour is asked for the Son.
vv: the Son can do nothing on his own, but only what he sees the Father doing;

This does not mean that the Son is lesser. Only one who shares the Father’s life can do “whatever the Father does”. The image of a son learning his father’s trade may stand behind the verse, but the claim goes far beyond it.
just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes.
The healing of the man at the pool was a sign of this. The “greater works” of v. 20 begin here and reach their end at the empty tomb.
so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.
No one can honour God rightly and put the Son aside: the verse says plainly that the two honours are one.
ch: The Church confesses the Son as “one in being with the Father” at the Council of Nicaea. St Augustine, preaching on this passage, taught that Father and Son do not do different works but the same works inseparably (Tractates on John 20; in substance). The Catechism teaches that the whole divine economy is the common work of the three divine persons (CCC 258), and that the Father “has given all judgment to the Son” (CCC 679, quoting John 5:22).

qa: If “the Son can do nothing on his own”, how can he be equal to the Father?

The verse speaks of origin, not of rank. All that the Son has he receives from the Father, from eternity, and he receives all of it. Because of that he does “whatever the Father does” (5:19). This is what the Church means in the Creed by “God from God, Light from Light”.
study: When has fear made me plan as though God were not there? What did it cost those near me?
Jesus lives by looking at the Father. What daily practice in this Great Fast helps me to look at him?
